parents.title: A guide for parents
parents.lead: How to set KidLearn up for your family, what your child will do in it, and how to keep an eye on how it is going.

start.title: Getting started
start.p1: You sign in with your Google account, so there is no separate password to remember. The first time, KidLearn asks for your permission before anything about your child is stored.
start.step1: Choose Parent sign-in on the homepage, then Continue with Google.
start.step2: Read what we keep and what we never do, then tick the box to confirm you are the child's parent or guardian.
start.step3: Add your first child. When you are done, you land on your profiles page.

child.title: Adding a child
child.p1: Each child has a profile with a first name, an age from three to six, a grade, a language and an avatar from a starter set. You can change any of these later under Children.
child.p2: You can add up to five children. To remove a child, you type their first name to confirm. Removing a child deletes all of their progress, rewards and reports.

day.title: Your child's day
day.intro: Your child taps their picture, picks a world and plays. Everything is spoken aloud, so a child who cannot read yet can still find their way.

lessons.p1: Every lesson follows the same five steps in the same order: a friendly mascot says what it is about, a short video of one to three minutes, a hands-on activity such as tracing a letter or matching pairs, a short quiz, and a celebration.
lessons.p2: Progress is saved after each step, so if the tablet runs out of battery your child picks up where they left off. The video has no controls to wander off with: no full screen, no download and no links.

quiz.p1: Three to five questions, one at a time, each read aloud. A single tap answers.
quiz.p2: A wrong answer fades gently and a warm voice encourages your child to try again. There is no buzzer, no red cross and no percentage, and the score screen always ends in praise.

stories.p1: A library of read-along picture stories, separate from the lessons. Every page is narrated, and pages turn by themselves after the narration, so the youngest children can simply listen.
stories.p2: Finishing a story earns a small reward the first time. Reading it again is always allowed, because reading the same story again builds fluency.

rewards.p1: Your child earns stars for finishing lessons and coins for right answers, collects badges for milestones and unlocks new characters. A streak counts the days in a row they have learned.
rewards.p2: Rewards are worked out on our server, not on the device, so they reflect real learning. Locked characters appear as friendly silhouettes: something to look forward to, never a punishment.

corner.title: Reaching the parent area from your child's screen
corner.p1: On your child's screens, a small button in the top corner leads to the parent area. On the screen where your child picks their profile, it shows your Google photo and name; everywhere else it is a plain lock. It is hidden during lessons and stories, so a child in the middle of one cannot tap out by accident.
corner.p2: There is no PIN: your Google sign-in is the lock. If your child uses a device you are signed in on, they can reach this area, so the actions that cannot be undone ask you to confirm first.
corner.p3: Inside the parent area, the account menu in the top bar takes you Back to kid mode or signs you out. Signing out also ends your child's session on that device.

progress.title: Following their progress
progress.intro: What you can see about each child, and the limits you can set.

dashboard.p2: A child who is just starting sees a friendly message instead of a row of zeros, and the strongest and needs-practice labels appear only once there is something to compare.
dashboard.p1: Progress shows one child at a time; switch between children with the tabs. You see their learning time today, this week and this month; their progress in each subject, with the subject they are strongest in and the one that needs practice; and their 20 most recent lessons, stories and badges.

reports.p1: For every week from Monday to Sunday, each child gets a report under Weekly report. It shows the days they were active, the minutes they spent learning, the new letters, words and numbers they met, the lessons and stories they finished, how often they answered quiz questions right first time, and the badges they earned. Earlier weeks are listed below the latest one.
reports.p2: Reports are shown in the app. They are not sent by email.

language.title: Language
language.p1: KidLearn works in English and Bangla. To switch the language of your own screens, use the button at the top of the parent area. Your choice is remembered on that device.
language.p2: Each child also has their own language, set on their profile. On the child's screens, the child's language wins, so one child can learn in Bangla while a brother or sister learns in English on the same tablet.

safety.title: Safety and privacy
safety.intro: KidLearn is made for young children. The rules below are enforced by the software itself, not only promised.

data.p2: Your child's profile and progress are visible only to you. Nothing about your child is shared with anyone else or used for advertising.
data.p1: We keep each child's first name, age, grade and avatar (no surname, no photo), their lesson progress, and your Google name and email. There are no ads, we never sell data, and there is no chat and nothing to buy. If that wording ever changes, we ask you again.

screens.p1: There is no chat, no messages, no comments and no public profile, so nobody can contact your child.
screens.p2: Your child's screens contain no links to other websites and nothing to buy. A test in our code fails if a link ever appears, even inside a lesson title.

content.p1: Our team writes lessons, stories and quizzes with the help of AI tools, which draft the text, narration and pictures in English and Bangla. Nothing an AI drafts reaches your child until a person on our team has read it and approved it.
content.p2: AI tools never see anything about your child or your family: they are given lesson topics and nothing else. Your child never talks to an AI in KidLearn.

delete.title: Deleting your account and data
delete.p1: Deleting your account erases everything: every child, all their progress and reports, your parent record and your sign-in. It happens in one step on our server, with no grace period and no copy kept, and it cannot be undone.
delete.p2: To make sure it is really you, it takes two steps: a request, then a confirmation within 15 minutes. The page for this is not in the web app yet. Until it is, you can delete each child under Children, which removes all of that child's data straight away.

wrongAnswer.term: What happens when my child gets an answer wrong?
wrongAnswer.detail: They try again. There is no buzzer, no score to lose and no way to fail a lesson.

twoChildren.term: Can two children share one tablet?
twoChildren.detail: Yes. Each child taps their own picture on the profile screen and keeps their own progress, rewards and language.

seeAi.term: Will my child talk to an AI?
seeAi.detail: No. AI only helps our team draft lessons, a person approves every one, and nothing about your child is ever sent to an AI.

offline.term: Does KidLearn work without the internet?
offline.detail: No. It needs a connection, because progress and rewards are recorded on our server. If the connection drops during a lesson, your child resumes from the last step they finished.

admins.title: A guide for content admins
admins.lead: The CMS is where lessons, stories and quizzes are written, drafted with AI, reviewed and published. One rule runs through all of it: nothing an AI drafts reaches a child until a person has approved it.

account.title: What an admin account is
account.p1: An admin signs in with an email address and password from Admin sign-in on the homepage. Parents sign in with Google. The two kinds of account never overlap, and a parent who opens an admin page is turned away.
account.p2: There is no sign-up page and no invitation. An engineer creates each admin account with a script: Part 1 of the admin account guide covers local development, and Part 2 covers a deployed server. A forgotten password is reset the same way.

workspace.title: The workspace
workspace.p1: The sidebar has six sections: Curriculum, Stories, Media, Badges, AI Queue and Analytics. You land on Analytics when you sign in, and AI Queue shows how many drafts are waiting for review. The CMS is designed for a desktop screen; on narrower screens the sidebar becomes a bar along the top.

curriculum.title: Building the curriculum
curriculum.p1: Content is organised as subjects, then topics, then lessons, shown side by side in three panes. You can drag to reorder at any level. A lesson's world, the setting a child sees it in, is a field on the lesson rather than another level.
curriculum.p2: Each lesson has an English tab and a Bangla tab, each with a title, intro and narration scripts, videos and grade levels, and links to one activity and one quiz. The quiz and activity editors check what you type as you go, and preview it with the same component a child will see.

media.title: Media
media.p1: Videos, audio and images upload straight from your browser to Cloudinary. No file passes through our server, which keeps only each file's address and details. You can attach media to lesson videos, story pictures, quiz questions, world mascots and badge icons.

ai.title: The AI pipeline
ai.p1: From the CMS you can ask for a draft lesson, story, set of quiz questions, narration or illustration. Text and images come from Google's Gemini models; narration comes from Google Cloud Text-to-Speech, with English and Bangla voices. Admins can also connect the AI assistant they already use — Claude, Cursor or VS Code — and let it write lessons, stories and quizzes on their own subscription.
ai.p2: Every draft is checked against the same rules that hand-written content must pass, then saved as a draft waiting for review. Each kind of draft has a daily limit, so one busy day cannot use up the whole budget.

review.title: The review queue
review.p1: Filter the queue by type, language or grade, then open a draft to read the text, listen to the audio and look at the pictures. You have three choices:
review.approve: Approve: it is published as it is.
review.edit: Edit, then approve: fix it in an editor that opens already filled in.
review.reject: Reject: give a reason of at least ten characters, so the next person knows why.
review.p2: A draft cannot be published while it still has a placeholder image. Every decision is recorded with who made it, when and why.

lifecycle.title: The publishing lifecycle
lifecycle.p1: All content, whether written by hand or drafted by AI, moves through the same statuses. Children only ever see published content.
lifecycle.p2: Rejected content cannot jump straight to published: it goes back to draft and through review again. Published content can be taken back to draft, and anything can be archived and restored later.

cannot.title: What an admin cannot do
cannot.p1: Some limits are deliberate. An admin cannot:
cannot.familyData: See any child's or parent's personal details. The CMS holds no family records, and Analytics shows totals only.
cannot.publish: Publish AI-drafted content without a review decision. The server refuses.
cannot.accounts: Create another admin, or reset a password, from the CMS.
cannot.google: Sign in with Google. That is for parents only.

engineering.title: How KidLearn is built
engineering.lead: The stack and the alternatives it beat, the architecture, how AI content is kept behind a human, and how it is tested and shipped. Every claim links to the document it comes from.

stack.title: The stack
stack.intro: One choice per layer. Each tab says what was picked, why, what it costs, and what it beat.

web.choice: Next.js 16 with the App Router, React 19 and Tailwind CSS v4.
web.why: Phones and tablets come first, so pages are built mobile-first. Design tokens live in CSS variables, which lets the kid theme and the parent theme share one set of components and swap at runtime without a line of theme logic in JavaScript.
web.tradeoff: Every route is rendered on demand, because the root layout reads the language cookie on the server. That trades static caching for a Bangla visitor never seeing a flash of English.
web.alternatives: A plain Vite single-page app (no server rendering, so a slow phone sees a blank screen longer) and Remix (fewer people know it, and Vercel hosts Next.js with no configuration).

api.choice: Express 5 in TypeScript (ESM), one module per domain.
api.why: A small, explicit REST API that is easy to read top to bottom. Every route that takes input checks it with the same Zod schemas that generate its OpenAPI document, and a test fails if any live route is missing from that document.
api.tradeoff: Express brings no structure of its own, so the conventions (routes, schema, service, middleware per module) are written down and enforced in review rather than by the framework.
api.alternatives: NestJS (more ceremony than a two-person API needs), Next.js route handlers (would tie the API to the web host and leave nothing for the planned mobile app to call) and tRPC (TypeScript-only, so no contract for a non-TypeScript client).

database.choice: PostgreSQL through Prisma 6, with JSONB for lesson content.
database.why: The family, progress and publishing data is relational and needs transactions and foreign keys. Lesson and quiz payloads change shape as new activity types arrive, so they live in versioned JSONB columns checked by Zod. Row-level security is on for every table, so Supabase's public Data API cannot reach around the server.
database.tradeoff: Prisma cannot type a JSONB column, so every payload is parsed at the edge of the service that reads it. Prisma's generated client also has to be built before the server type-checks.
database.alternatives: MongoDB (would give up the transactions that award stars and delete a family in one step) and Drizzle (closer to SQL, but Prisma's migrations and schema file were the better fit for a schema that changes often).

auth.choice: better-auth: Google sign-in for parents, email and password for admins.
auth.why: Parents never create a password, and Google handles account recovery. Admins cannot sign up at all: the only way to create one is a seed script run on the server. An admin session ends 12 hours after sign-in however active it is, while a parent's slides for 30 days.
auth.tradeoff: Parents without a Google account cannot sign in. Account linking is switched off on purpose, so a Google sign-in on an admin's address can never inherit the admin account.
auth.alternatives: Auth.js (built around Next.js, but the sessions belong to the Express API) and a hosted service such as Clerk or Auth0 (a monthly bill and child-adjacent data held by a third party).

media.choice: Cloudinary, uploaded straight from the browser with a signed request.
media.why: The API signs an upload and the browser sends the file directly to Cloudinary, so no image or audio clip passes through the API's memory. Cloudinary resizes and serves images from its CDN, and the free plan covers the expected traffic.
media.tradeoff: Another vendor with its own dashboard and keys, and a URL format the app depends on.
media.alternatives: Amazon S3 with CloudFront (cheaper at scale, but image resizing would have to be built) and Supabase Storage (fewer vendors, but no on-the-fly transformations on the free tier).

hosting.choice: Vercel for the web app; one EC2 instance running Docker Compose behind Caddy for the API (planned).
hosting.why: The production and development APIs run side by side on one Graviton instance in Mumbai, close to Bangladesh. Caddy handles TLS and is the only process listening on the public ports. The estimated cost for both environments is about $14.08 a month.
hosting.tradeoff: One instance is one point of failure, and there is no autoscaling. That is accepted for now: rollback is one command, and the database lives elsewhere.
hosting.alternatives: ECS or App Runner behind a load balancer (the load balancer alone would cost more each month than the instance) and running the API on Vercel too (long AI generation requests and the weekly report job do not fit serverless limits).

architecture.title: Architecture
architecture.intro: The shape of the system: how the code is organised, how a request travels, and the rules that keep content and rewards honest.

monorepo.choice: One pnpm workspace built with Turborepo: two apps and six packages.
monorepo.why: Types, strings, design tokens and the database client are shared, so a change to an API contract breaks the web app's type-check in the same pull request. Dependencies point one way: apps import packages, never the reverse.
monorepo.tradeoff: One lockfile and one CI job for everything, so a slow test anywhere slows every pull request. packages/ui is web-only by decision, because its Radix primitives need a browser DOM.
monorepo.alternatives: Separate repositories for web and API (contracts would drift between releases) and Nx (more features than two apps need).

request.choice: The browser calls the API directly, with an httpOnly session cookie on the API's own origin.
request.why: There is no proxy in between. Express refuses any state-changing request from an origin other than the web app's, guards such as requireParent and requireAdmin check the session before a handler runs, and requireConsent holds back child data until a parent has agreed. Prisma is the only way into the database.
request.tradeoff: The web app and the API need CORS and a cookie set up carefully across two hostnames, and the web app has exactly one allowed origin per environment.
request.alternatives: Proxying every call through Next.js (one more hop and a second place to get auth wrong) and tokens in local storage (readable by any script on the page).

content.choice: Activities and quizzes are versioned JSONB payloads, drawn by generic engines in the web app.
content.why: Drag and drop, tracing, matching, puzzles and quiz questions are each described by a payload with a schemaVersion. One set of Zod schemas in packages/types checks a payload when an admin saves it, when an AI drafts it, and when the app reads it. A new lesson is data, not code, and goes live without a deploy.
content.tradeoff: A new kind of activity still needs code: a schema and an engine. Older payloads have to be migrated as they are read, so every write can stay strict.
content.alternatives: A React component per lesson (every lesson would need a deploy) and a headless CMS (no way to check that a lesson actually plays).

authority.choice: Stars, streaks, learning time and lesson completion are worked out on the server.
authority.why: The app reports what happened, such as a finished step or a heartbeat while a lesson is open, and the server decides what it means. It enforces step order, rate-limits reports, and pays nothing for a lesson until the steps that prove it are on record. Learning time is added up from session events, so there is no counter for a device to inflate.
authority.tradeoff: Every reward waits on a round trip, so the app shows the celebration while the server confirms it, and offline play cannot earn anything.
authority.alternatives: Counting on the device and syncing later (easy to cheat, and learning time would only be as honest as the tablet's clock).

ai.title: AI content
ai.intro: AI drafts lessons, stories, quizzes, narration and pictures. It reaches a child only after a person approves it.

overview.choice: Two doors in, one gate out.
overview.why: AI content enters through Gemini, run by KidLearn, or through an admin's own assistant over MCP. Both doors share the same prompts, the same Zod schemas and the same save path, and both end in the same review queue. Every generation keeps an audit trail: inputs, prompts, raw attempts, token use, who asked and who approved.
overview.tradeoff: Two code paths to keep consistent. Sharing the rule book, the schemas and the persistence keeps the difference to who writes the JSON.
overview.alternatives: Gemini only (admins with their own subscription would be limited to a small daily budget) and MCP only (admins without an AI subscription could not generate anything).

gemini.choice: Door 1: a Generate button in the CMS that calls Gemini with KidLearn's key.
gemini.why: Gemini returns structured JSON that is checked against the same Zod schema the game engines read. A first attempt that fails validation is retried once with the errors as feedback; a second failure ends the job. Daily budgets per kind of job keep the bill predictable.
gemini.tradeoff: The admin waits while the model works, because jobs run in the request rather than on a queue. A busy day hits the budget and has to wait for tomorrow.
gemini.alternatives: A job queue with workers (more infrastructure than three jobs a day need) and free-form text parsed afterwards (content the engines could not trust).

mcp.choice: Door 2: KidLearn is an MCP server, and an admin's own assistant writes the drafts.
mcp.why: Admins already pay for Claude, Cursor or Gemini CLI, and in a chat they can ask for changes before submitting. The assistant runs the model on the admin's subscription, so KidLearn holds no text-model key for this door. An admin signs the assistant in with a personal token that can write drafts and nothing else: it can never approve, publish, edit or delete.
mcp.tradeoff: KidLearn cannot configure an outside model's safety filters or its Bangla, so for this door the human reviewer is the only safety gate KidLearn controls.
mcp.alternatives: OAuth for MCP clients (not yet supported by the desktop clients admins use) and one shared API key (no way to tell who submitted a draft or to revoke one person).

media.choice: Narration from Google Cloud Text-to-Speech, illustrations from Gemini's image model, both made on the server.
media.why: One voice per language keeps narration consistent. Recurring characters keep their look through written character sheets added to every illustration prompt. Media is generated on the server even for MCP drafts, so the server never fetches an image from an address an outside model chose.
media.tradeoff: Character sheets are text, so a character can still drift between pictures, and the reviewer catches it. Pictures need a Gemini key or a manual upload.
media.alternatives: Accepting image URLs from MCP clients (opens the server to request forgery) and recording narration by hand (slow for two languages).

review.choice: Nothing an AI makes reaches a child until an admin approves it.
review.why: Every generator writes draft rows, and a job can only end as awaiting_review or failed. Approving checks for blockers, then walks the content to published. The publish check itself refuses AI content without an approved job, even through the ordinary CMS. Child and parent data never reaches a model.
review.tradeoff: Content arrives only as fast as people can review it.
review.alternatives: Automatic publishing behind safety filters (for children aged three to six, a filter is not enough on its own).

social.detail: No chat, no messages and no public profiles. Nobody can contact a child.

links.term: No way out of the child's screens
links.detail: The child's screens contain no external links, and a test fails if one appears, even inside a lesson title written in the CMS.

consent.detail: The server refuses to create a child profile or record progress until a parent has given consent.

aiData.term: No family data in AI prompts
aiData.detail: Prompts carry curriculum text and the admin's request, nothing else. A test asserts that no MCP tool can read child, parent, progress or account data.

deletion.detail: Deleting an account erases everything about the family in one database transaction. There is no soft delete and no grace period.

quality.title: Quality and shipping
quality.intro: How a change is checked before it merges, and how it reaches production.

tooling.choice: Biome for lint and formatting, TypeScript in strict mode everywhere.
tooling.why: One fast tool lints, formats and sorts imports across the whole repository, so there is no ESLint and Prettier configuration to keep in step. tsc type-checks every package with no implicit any.
tooling.tradeoff: Biome has fewer rules and plugins than ESLint, and it does not catch Tailwind class issues; the editor's Tailwind extension does.
tooling.alternatives: ESLint with Prettier (two tools, two configurations, and several times slower on a monorepo).

tests.choice: Vitest in every package, contract checks on every route, and a real Postgres for what a stub cannot prove.
tests.why: Every successful response in a route test is checked against its published schema with assertContract. Cascades, unique constraints and the status check on related rows run against a real database in *.db.test.ts suites, which refuse any database not named *_test.
tests.tradeoff: Most server suites stub Prisma for speed, so they need care to stay honest; the rules for a new stubbed suite are written down.
tests.alternatives: Only end-to-end browser tests (slow and flaky as the main suite) and a mocked database everywhere (would miss the constraints the data depends on).

ci.choice: GitHub Actions, one required job called gates.
ci.why: On every pull request and every push to main or dev: install from the lockfile, lint, build, type-check, the tests with coverage, and the real-database suites against a Postgres service. Both branches require a pull request and a green gates.
ci.tradeoff: Coverage is reported but deliberately not gated on a threshold, so it relies on review.
ci.alternatives: Several smaller jobs (more parallel, but more places to read when something fails) and a coverage gate (encourages tests written for the number).

releases.choice: Images tagged by commit, a deploy script with health gates, and migrations only on request.
releases.why: One image serves both environments, configured at runtime. deploy.sh waits for the healthcheck and a database read before it counts a deploy as good, and remembers the last good tag for rollback. Database migrations run only when the deploy asks for them, so a schema change is a decision, not a side effect of a restart.
releases.tradeoff: Deploys are run by hand for now; a GitHub Actions deploy pipeline is specified but not yet built.
releases.alternatives: Kubernetes (far more than one instance needs) and running migrations on every start (one bad restart could change the schema).

monorepo.title: Workspace dependency diagram: apps/web imports packages/ui, i18n and types; apps/server imports db and types; the planned apps/mobile will import i18n, tokens and types; ui imports tokens; i18n and db import types.
monorepo.caption: What imports what. The packages also share tsconfig bases from packages/config.

request.title: Request path diagram: the browser loads pages from Next.js on Vercel, then calls the API directly with its session cookie; Caddy passes the call to Express on EC2, which checks the session, then reaches PostgreSQL through Prisma.
request.caption: Pages come from Vercel; data comes straight from the API.

lifecycle.title: Publishing lifecycle diagram: draft goes to in_review on submit; in_review goes to approved when a person approves, or to rejected; approved goes to published; rejected goes back to draft for rework.
lifecycle.caption: Only published content reaches a child.
